She had been diagnosed with AF 3 months prior and was prescribed flecainide, 100 mg twice daily; metoprolol; and apixaban. She was also taking furosemide, 40 mg twice daily. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60%, mild mitral regurgitation, and grade 2 diastolic dysfunction. An electrocardiogram (ECG) obtained 1 month before presentation showed sinus rhythm, PR interval of 190 milliseconds, and QRS interval of 100 milliseconds. On presentation, she was anxious appearing, mildly dyspneic, and tachycardic, with a heart rate of 130 bpm. Blood pressure was 94/52 mm Hg. Her mentation was normal, and she denied chest pain. Initial ECG (Figure 1) showed a monomorphic, wide complex tachycardia at 130 bpm with a QRS duration of 220 milliseconds and right bundle branch morphology. Laboratory testing was notable for acute kidney injury, with a creatinine level of 4.0 mg/dL (baseline, 1.4 mg/dL; to convert to micromoles per liter, multiply by 88.4) (estimated glomerular filtration rate, 12 mL/min/1.73 m2); troponin I, 0.029 ng/mL (reference range, <0.04 ng/mL; to convert to micrograms per liter, multiply by 1); sodium, 132 mEq/L (to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 1); potassium, 5.1 mEq/L (to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 1); and normal values of serum magnesium, calcium, and phosphorus.

case_info.explanation: Atrial flutter with 2:1 atrioventricular block, and severe intraventricular conduction delay due to flecainide toxicity D. Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate Flecainide is a class Ic antiarrhythmic drug. It delays phase 0 depolarization of the action potential by blocking cardiac voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.5, resulting in slowing of conduction.1,2Its major use is in the treatment and prevention of symptomatic AF and supraventricular tachycardias. Contraindications include bundle branch block, cardiomyopathies, and significant liver or kidney impairment. The usual dose of flecainide is 50 to 150 mg every 12 hours. The half-life is 12 to 27 hours. It undergoes hepatic oxidation by cytochrome P450 (CYP2D6 isoform); however, approximately 80% of clearance is by the kidneys; thus, dosing must be reduced to 50 mg twice daily if there is kidney failure.3Notably, hemodialysis is not an effective method for clearance due to the large volume of distribution.4Aside from kidney and liver failure, toxic effects can occur with hypovolemia, hypokalemia, and hyponatremia and in patients who carry alleles that decrease their ability to metabolize CYP2D. Acute toxic effects can present with dizziness, seizures, visual disturbance, sinus arrest, atrioventricular (AV) block, and ventricular tachyarrhythmias.5Toxic effects should be suspected if the QRS duration increases by 50% or if the PR interval increases by 30%.6Prominent terminal R waves (≥3 mm) in lead aVR are a sensitive predictor of toxic effects (Figure 1).7Treatment of hemodynamically unstable tachyarrhythmias should include cardioversion. Amiodarone may be used to suppress ventricular tachycardia (VT). Bradyarrhythmias may require transvenous pacing. Closer inspection of this patient’s ECG on admission at our hospital (Figure 2) showed that the rhythm was atrial flutter (AFL) with an atrial cycle length of 230 milliseconds and 2:1 AV conduction. Flecainide slows atrial conduction, thereby slowing the rate of AFL (typically approximately 300 bpm) as seen in this patient (to approximately 260 bpm), and, if not given concomitantly with a β-blocker, may result in 1:1 AV nodal conduction resulting in ventricular fibrillation. The differential diagnosis of a wide complex tachycardia with flecainide use includes supraventricular tachycardia (including AFL) with 1:1 or 2:1 block and aberrancy, intraventricular conduction delay (IVCD), preexcitation, and VT.8 Mortality due to flecainide toxicity may be as high as 22%. The mainstay of treatment is sodium bicarbonate administration to reverse the sodium channel blockade through competitive inhibition and to alkalize the serum pH, which facilitates flecainide dissociation from its sodium channel binding sites; the pH goal should be 7.55, and the serum sodium level should be 150 mEq/L.4,9The dose is a 1-mEq/kg bolus followed by an infusion of 15 to 20 mEq/h. In refractory cases, intravenous lipid emulsion therapy may be tried—this serves as a “lipid sink” to remove lipophilic drugs, such as flecainide, from the circulation. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation may be needed in profound shock. The patient was treated with sodium bicarbonate. The QRS interval progressively narrowed with the rhythm first changing to AF and then spontaneously reverting to sinus rhythm, PR interval of 195 milliseconds, nonspecific IVCD (QRS interval of 112 milliseconds), and prolonged QTc interval (504 milliseconds). A serum flecainide measurement ordered on admission was available on day 2 and was 1.42 μg/mL (reference range, 0.2-0.9 μg/mL); the serum creatinine level improved to 1.6 mg/dL after intravenous fluids were administered. She was discharged on hospital day 3 and was doing well at 1-month follow-up. If AF recurs, she has opted for catheter ablation.

   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be

     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

     message imposes on YOU.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

case_info.explanation: Atrial flutter with 2:1 atrioventricular block, and severe intraventricular conduction delay due to flecainide toxicity D. Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate Flecainide is a class Ic antiarrhythmic drug. It delays phase 0 depolarization of the action potential by blocking cardiac voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.5, resulting in slowing of conduction.1,2Its major use is in the treatment and prevention of symptomatic AF and supraventricular tachycardias. Contraindications include bundle branch block, cardiomyopathies, and significant liver or kidney impairment. The usual dose of flecainide is 50 to 150 mg every 12 hours. The half-life is 12 to 27 hours. It undergoes hepatic oxidation by cytochrome P450 (CYP2D6 isoform); however, approximately 80% of clearance is by the kidneys; thus, dosing must be reduced to 50 mg twice daily if there is kidney failure.3Notably, hemodialysis is not an effective method for clearance due to the large volume of distribution.4Aside from kidney and liver failure, toxic effects can occur with hypovolemia, hypokalemia, and hyponatremia and in patients who carry alleles that decrease their ability to metabolize CYP2D. Acute toxic effects can present with dizziness, seizures, visual disturbance, sinus arrest, atrioventricular (AV) block, and ventricular tachyarrhythmias.5Toxic effects should be suspected if the QRS duration increases by 50% or if the PR interval increases by 30%.6Prominent terminal R waves (≥3 mm) in lead aVR are a sensitive predictor of toxic effects (Figure 1).7Treatment of hemodynamically unstable tachyarrhythmias should include cardioversion. Amiodarone may be used to suppress ventricular tachycardia (VT). Bradyarrhythmias may require transvenous pacing. Closer inspection of this patient’s ECG on admission at our hospital (Figure 2) showed that the rhythm was atrial flutter (AFL) with an atrial cycle length of 230 milliseconds and 2:1 AV conduction. Flecainide slows atrial conduction, thereby slowing the rate of AFL (typically approximately 300 bpm) as seen in this patient (to approximately 260 bpm), and, if not given concomitantly with a β-blocker, may result in 1:1 AV nodal conduction resulting in ventricular fibrillation. The differential diagnosis of a wide complex tachycardia with flecainide use includes supraventricular tachycardia (including AFL) with 1:1 or 2:1 block and aberrancy, intraventricular conduction delay (IVCD), preexcitation, and VT.8 Mortality due to flecainide toxicity may be as high as 22%. The mainstay of treatment is sodium bicarbonate administration to reverse the sodium channel blockade through competitive inhibition and to alkalize the serum pH, which facilitates flecainide dissociation from its sodium channel binding sites; the pH goal should be 7.55, and the serum sodium level should be 150 mEq/L.4,9The dose is a 1-mEq/kg bolus followed by an infusion of 15 to 20 mEq/h. In refractory cases, intravenous lipid emulsion therapy may be tried—this serves as a “lipid sink” to remove lipophilic drugs, such as flecainide, from the circulation. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation may be needed in profound shock. The patient was treated with sodium bicarbonate. The QRS interval progressively narrowed with the rhythm first changing to AF and then spontaneously reverting to sinus rhythm, PR interval of 195 milliseconds, nonspecific IVCD (QRS interval of 112 milliseconds), and prolonged QTc interval (504 milliseconds). A serum flecainide measurement ordered on admission was available on day 2 and was 1.42 μg/mL (reference range, 0.2-0.9 μg/mL); the serum creatinine level improved to 1.6 mg/dL after intravenous fluids were administered. She was discharged on hospital day 3 and was doing well at 1-month follow-up. If AF recurs, she has opted for catheter ablation.

       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,

       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Atrial flutter with 2:1 atrioventricular block, and severe intraventricular conduction delay due to flecainide toxicity D. Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate Flecainide is a class Ic antiarrhythmic drug. It delays phase 0 depolarization of the action potential by blocking cardiac voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.5, resulting in slowing of conduction.1,2Its major use is in the treatment and prevention of symptomatic AF and supraventricular tachycardias. Contraindications include bundle branch block, cardiomyopathies, and significant liver or kidney impairment. The usual dose of flecainide is 50 to 150 mg every 12 hours. The half-life is 12 to 27 hours. It undergoes hepatic oxidation by cytochrome P450 (CYP2D6 isoform); however, approximately 80% of clearance is by the kidneys; thus, dosing must be reduced to 50 mg twice daily if there is kidney failure.3Notably, hemodialysis is not an effective method for clearance due to the large volume of distribution.4Aside from kidney and liver failure, toxic effects can occur with hypovolemia, hypokalemia, and hyponatremia and in patients who carry alleles that decrease their ability to metabolize CYP2D. Acute toxic effects can present with dizziness, seizures, visual disturbance, sinus arrest, atrioventricular (AV) block, and ventricular tachyarrhythmias.5Toxic effects should be suspected if the QRS duration increases by 50% or if the PR interval increases by 30%.6Prominent terminal R waves (≥3 mm) in lead aVR are a sensitive predictor of toxic effects (Figure 1).7Treatment of hemodynamically unstable tachyarrhythmias should include cardioversion. Amiodarone may be used to suppress ventricular tachycardia (VT). Bradyarrhythmias may require transvenous pacing. Closer inspection of this patient’s ECG on admission at our hospital (Figure 2) showed that the rhythm was atrial flutter (AFL) with an atrial cycle length of 230 milliseconds and 2:1 AV conduction. Flecainide slows atrial conduction, thereby slowing the rate of AFL (typically approximately 300 bpm) as seen in this patient (to approximately 260 bpm), and, if not given concomitantly with a β-blocker, may result in 1:1 AV nodal conduction resulting in ventricular fibrillation. The differential diagnosis of a wide complex tachycardia with flecainide use includes supraventricular tachycardia (including AFL) with 1:1 or 2:1 block and aberrancy, intraventricular conduction delay (IVCD), preexcitation, and VT.8 Mortality due to flecainide toxicity may be as high as 22%. The mainstay of treatment is sodium bicarbonate administration to reverse the sodium channel blockade through competitive inhibition and to alkalize the serum pH, which facilitates flecainide dissociation from its sodium channel binding sites; the pH goal should be 7.55, and the serum sodium level should be 150 mEq/L.4,9The dose is a 1-mEq/kg bolus followed by an infusion of 15 to 20 mEq/h. In refractory cases, intravenous lipid emulsion therapy may be tried—this serves as a “lipid sink” to remove lipophilic drugs, such as flecainide, from the circulation. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation may be needed in profound shock. The patient was treated with sodium bicarbonate. The QRS interval progressively narrowed with the rhythm first changing to AF and then spontaneously reverting to sinus rhythm, PR interval of 195 milliseconds, nonspecific IVCD (QRS interval of 112 milliseconds), and prolonged QTc interval (504 milliseconds). A serum flecainide measurement ordered on admission was available on day 2 and was 1.42 μg/mL (reference range, 0.2-0.9 μg/mL); the serum creatinine level improved to 1.6 mg/dL after intravenous fluids were administered. She was discharged on hospital day 3 and was doing well at 1-month follow-up. If AF recurs, she has opted for catheter ablation.

case_info.explanation: Atrial flutter with 2:1 atrioventricular block, and severe intraventricular conduction delay due to flecainide toxicity D. Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate Flecainide is a class Ic antiarrhythmic drug. It delays phase 0 depolarization of the action potential by blocking cardiac voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.5, resulting in slowing of conduction.1,2Its major use is in the treatment and prevention of symptomatic AF and supraventricular tachycardias. Contraindications include bundle branch block, cardiomyopathies, and significant liver or kidney impairment. The usual dose of flecainide is 50 to 150 mg every 12 hours. The half-life is 12 to 27 hours. It undergoes hepatic oxidation by cytochrome P450 (CYP2D6 isoform); however, approximately 80% of clearance is by the kidneys; thus, dosing must be reduced to 50 mg twice daily if there is kidney failure.3Notably, hemodialysis is not an effective method for clearance due to the large volume of distribution.4Aside from kidney and liver failure, toxic effects can occur with hypovolemia, hypokalemia, and hyponatremia and in patients who carry alleles that decrease their ability to metabolize CYP2D. Acute toxic effects can present with dizziness, seizures, visual disturbance, sinus arrest, atrioventricular (AV) block, and ventricular tachyarrhythmias.5Toxic effects should be suspected if the QRS duration increases by 50% or if the PR interval increases by 30%.6Prominent terminal R waves (≥3 mm) in lead aVR are a sensitive predictor of toxic effects (Figure 1).7Treatment of hemodynamically unstable tachyarrhythmias should include cardioversion. Amiodarone may be used to suppress ventricular tachycardia (VT). Bradyarrhythmias may require transvenous pacing. Closer inspection of this patient’s ECG on admission at our hospital (Figure 2) showed that the rhythm was atrial flutter (AFL) with an atrial cycle length of 230 milliseconds and 2:1 AV conduction. Flecainide slows atrial conduction, thereby slowing the rate of AFL (typically approximately 300 bpm) as seen in this patient (to approximately 260 bpm), and, if not given concomitantly with a β-blocker, may result in 1:1 AV nodal conduction resulting in ventricular fibrillation. The differential diagnosis of a wide complex tachycardia with flecainide use includes supraventricular tachycardia (including AFL) with 1:1 or 2:1 block and aberrancy, intraventricular conduction delay (IVCD), preexcitation, and VT.8 Mortality due to flecainide toxicity may be as high as 22%. The mainstay of treatment is sodium bicarbonate administration to reverse the sodium channel blockade through competitive inhibition and to alkalize the serum pH, which facilitates flecainide dissociation from its sodium channel binding sites; the pH goal should be 7.55, and the serum sodium level should be 150 mEq/L.4,9The dose is a 1-mEq/kg bolus followed by an infusion of 15 to 20 mEq/h. In refractory cases, intravenous lipid emulsion therapy may be tried—this serves as a “lipid sink” to remove lipophilic drugs, such as flecainide, from the circulation. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation may be needed in profound shock. The patient was treated with sodium bicarbonate. The QRS interval progressively narrowed with the rhythm first changing to AF and then spontaneously reverting to sinus rhythm, PR interval of 195 milliseconds, nonspecific IVCD (QRS interval of 112 milliseconds), and prolonged QTc interval (504 milliseconds). A serum flecainide measurement ordered on admission was available on day 2 and was 1.42 μg/mL (reference range, 0.2-0.9 μg/mL); the serum creatinine level improved to 1.6 mg/dL after intravenous fluids were administered. She was discharged on hospital day 3 and was doing well at 1-month follow-up. If AF recurs, she has opted for catheter ablation.

case_info.explanation: Atrial flutter with 2:1 atrioventricular block, and severe intraventricular conduction delay due to flecainide toxicity D. Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate Flecainide is a class Ic antiarrhythmic drug. It delays phase 0 depolarization of the action potential by blocking cardiac voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.5, resulting in slowing of conduction.1,2Its major use is in the treatment and prevention of symptomatic AF and supraventricular tachycardias. Contraindications include bundle branch block, cardiomyopathies, and significant liver or kidney impairment. The usual dose of flecainide is 50 to 150 mg every 12 hours. The half-life is 12 to 27 hours. It undergoes hepatic oxidation by cytochrome P450 (CYP2D6 isoform); however, approximately 80% of clearance is by the kidneys; thus, dosing must be reduced to 50 mg twice daily if there is kidney failure.3Notably, hemodialysis is not an effective method for clearance due to the large volume of distribution.4Aside from kidney and liver failure, toxic effects can occur with hypovolemia, hypokalemia, and hyponatremia and in patients who carry alleles that decrease their ability to metabolize CYP2D. Acute toxic effects can present with dizziness, seizures, visual disturbance, sinus arrest, atrioventricular (AV) block, and ventricular tachyarrhythmias.5Toxic effects should be suspected if the QRS duration increases by 50% or if the PR interval increases by 30%.6Prominent terminal R waves (≥3 mm) in lead aVR are a sensitive predictor of toxic effects (Figure 1).7Treatment of hemodynamically unstable tachyarrhythmias should include cardioversion. Amiodarone may be used to suppress ventricular tachycardia (VT). Bradyarrhythmias may require transvenous pacing. Closer inspection of this patient’s ECG on admission at our hospital (Figure 2) showed that the rhythm was atrial flutter (AFL) with an atrial cycle length of 230 milliseconds and 2:1 AV conduction. Flecainide slows atrial conduction, thereby slowing the rate of AFL (typically approximately 300 bpm) as seen in this patient (to approximately 260 bpm), and, if not given concomitantly with a β-blocker, may result in 1:1 AV nodal conduction resulting in ventricular fibrillation. The differential diagnosis of a wide complex tachycardia with flecainide use includes supraventricular tachycardia (including AFL) with 1:1 or 2:1 block and aberrancy, intraventricular conduction delay (IVCD), preexcitation, and VT.8 Mortality due to flecainide toxicity may be as high as 22%. The mainstay of treatment is sodium bicarbonate administration to reverse the sodium channel blockade through competitive inhibition and to alkalize the serum pH, which facilitates flecainide dissociation from its sodium channel binding sites; the pH goal should be 7.55, and the serum sodium level should be 150 mEq/L.4,9The dose is a 1-mEq/kg bolus followed by an infusion of 15 to 20 mEq/h. In refractory cases, intravenous lipid emulsion therapy may be tried—this serves as a “lipid sink” to remove lipophilic drugs, such as flecainide, from the circulation. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation may be needed in profound shock. The patient was treated with sodium bicarbonate. The QRS interval progressively narrowed with the rhythm first changing to AF and then spontaneously reverting to sinus rhythm, PR interval of 195 milliseconds, nonspecific IVCD (QRS interval of 112 milliseconds), and prolonged QTc interval (504 milliseconds). A serum flecainide measurement ordered on admission was available on day 2 and was 1.42 μg/mL (reference range, 0.2-0.9 μg/mL); the serum creatinine level improved to 1.6 mg/dL after intravenous fluids were administered. She was discharged on hospital day 3 and was doing well at 1-month follow-up. If AF recurs, she has opted for catheter ablation.

4. Frustration

case_info.explanation: Atrial flutter with 2:1 atrioventricular block, and severe intraventricular conduction delay due to flecainide toxicity D. Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate Flecainide is a class Ic antiarrhythmic drug. It delays phase 0 depolarization of the action potential by blocking cardiac voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.5, resulting in slowing of conduction.1,2Its major use is in the treatment and prevention of symptomatic AF and supraventricular tachycardias. Contraindications include bundle branch block, cardiomyopathies, and significant liver or kidney impairment. The usual dose of flecainide is 50 to 150 mg every 12 hours. The half-life is 12 to 27 hours. It undergoes hepatic oxidation by cytochrome P450 (CYP2D6 isoform); however, approximately 80% of clearance is by the kidneys; thus, dosing must be reduced to 50 mg twice daily if there is kidney failure.3Notably, hemodialysis is not an effective method for clearance due to the large volume of distribution.4Aside from kidney and liver failure, toxic effects can occur with hypovolemia, hypokalemia, and hyponatremia and in patients who carry alleles that decrease their ability to metabolize CYP2D. Acute toxic effects can present with dizziness, seizures, visual disturbance, sinus arrest, atrioventricular (AV) block, and ventricular tachyarrhythmias.5Toxic effects should be suspected if the QRS duration increases by 50% or if the PR interval increases by 30%.6Prominent terminal R waves (≥3 mm) in lead aVR are a sensitive predictor of toxic effects (Figure 1).7Treatment of hemodynamically unstable tachyarrhythmias should include cardioversion. Amiodarone may be used to suppress ventricular tachycardia (VT). Bradyarrhythmias may require transvenous pacing. Closer inspection of this patient’s ECG on admission at our hospital (Figure 2) showed that the rhythm was atrial flutter (AFL) with an atrial cycle length of 230 milliseconds and 2:1 AV conduction. Flecainide slows atrial conduction, thereby slowing the rate of AFL (typically approximately 300 bpm) as seen in this patient (to approximately 260 bpm), and, if not given concomitantly with a β-blocker, may result in 1:1 AV nodal conduction resulting in ventricular fibrillation. The differential diagnosis of a wide complex tachycardia with flecainide use includes supraventricular tachycardia (including AFL) with 1:1 or 2:1 block and aberrancy, intraventricular conduction delay (IVCD), preexcitation, and VT.8 Mortality due to flecainide toxicity may be as high as 22%. The mainstay of treatment is sodium bicarbonate administration to reverse the sodium channel blockade through competitive inhibition and to alkalize the serum pH, which facilitates flecainide dissociation from its sodium channel binding sites; the pH goal should be 7.55, and the serum sodium level should be 150 mEq/L.4,9The dose is a 1-mEq/kg bolus followed by an infusion of 15 to 20 mEq/h. In refractory cases, intravenous lipid emulsion therapy may be tried—this serves as a “lipid sink” to remove lipophilic drugs, such as flecainide, from the circulation. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation may be needed in profound shock. The patient was treated with sodium bicarbonate. The QRS interval progressively narrowed with the rhythm first changing to AF and then spontaneously reverting to sinus rhythm, PR interval of 195 milliseconds, nonspecific IVCD (QRS interval of 112 milliseconds), and prolonged QTc interval (504 milliseconds). A serum flecainide measurement ordered on admission was available on day 2 and was 1.42 μg/mL (reference range, 0.2-0.9 μg/mL); the serum creatinine level improved to 1.6 mg/dL after intravenous fluids were administered. She was discharged on hospital day 3 and was doing well at 1-month follow-up. If AF recurs, she has opted for catheter ablation.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully

She had been diagnosed with AF 3 months prior and was prescribed flecainide, 100 mg twice daily; metoprolol; and apixaban. She was also taking furosemide, 40 mg twice daily. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60%, mild mitral regurgitation, and grade 2 diastolic dysfunction. An electrocardiogram (ECG) obtained 1 month before presentation showed sinus rhythm, PR interval of 190 milliseconds, and QRS interval of 100 milliseconds. On presentation, she was anxious appearing, mildly dyspneic, and tachycardic, with a heart rate of 130 bpm. Blood pressure was 94/52 mm Hg. Her mentation was normal, and she denied chest pain. case_info.explanation: Atrial flutter with 2:1 atrioventricular block, and severe intraventricular conduction delay due to flecainide toxicity D. Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate Flecainide is a class Ic antiarrhythmic drug. It delays phase 0 depolarization of the action potential by blocking cardiac voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.5, resulting in slowing of conduction.1,2Its major use is in the treatment and prevention of symptomatic AF and supraventricular tachycardias. Contraindications include bundle branch block, cardiomyopathies, and significant liver or kidney impairment. The usual dose of flecainide is 50 to 150 mg every 12 hours. The half-life is 12 to 27 hours. It undergoes hepatic oxidation by cytochrome P450 (CYP2D6 isoform); however, approximately 80% of clearance is by the kidneys; thus, dosing must be reduced to 50 mg twice daily if there is kidney failure.3Notably, hemodialysis is not an effective method for clearance due to the large volume of distribution.4Aside from kidney and liver failure, toxic effects can occur with hypovolemia, hypokalemia, and hyponatremia and in patients who carry alleles that decrease their ability to metabolize CYP2D. Acute toxic effects can present with dizziness, seizures, visual disturbance, sinus arrest, atrioventricular (AV) block, and ventricular tachyarrhythmias.5Toxic effects should be suspected if the QRS duration increases by 50% or if the PR interval increases by 30%.6Prominent terminal R waves (≥3 mm) in lead aVR are a sensitive predictor of toxic effects (Figure 1).7Treatment of hemodynamically unstable tachyarrhythmias should include cardioversion. Amiodarone may be used to suppress ventricular tachycardia (VT). Bradyarrhythmias may require transvenous pacing. Closer inspection of this patient’s ECG on admission at our hospital (Figure 2) showed that the rhythm was atrial flutter (AFL) with an atrial cycle length of 230 milliseconds and 2:1 AV conduction. Flecainide slows atrial conduction, thereby slowing the rate of AFL (typically approximately 300 bpm) as seen in this patient (to approximately 260 bpm), and, if not given concomitantly with a β-blocker, may result in 1:1 AV nodal conduction resulting in ventricular fibrillation. The differential diagnosis of a wide complex tachycardia with flecainide use includes supraventricular tachycardia (including AFL) with 1:1 or 2:1 block and aberrancy, intraventricular conduction delay (IVCD), preexcitation, and VT.8 Mortality due to flecainide toxicity may be as high as 22%. The mainstay of treatment is sodium bicarbonate administration to reverse the sodium channel blockade through competitive inhibition and to alkalize the serum pH, which facilitates flecainide dissociation from its sodium channel binding sites; the pH goal should be 7.55, and the serum sodium level should be 150 mEq/L.4,9The dose is a 1-mEq/kg bolus followed by an infusion of 15 to 20 mEq/h. In refractory cases, intravenous lipid emulsion therapy may be tried—this serves as a “lipid sink” to remove lipophilic drugs, such as flecainide, from the circulation. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation may be needed in profound shock. The patient was treated with sodium bicarbonate. The QRS interval progressively narrowed with the rhythm first changing to AF and then spontaneously reverting to sinus rhythm, PR interval of 195 milliseconds, nonspecific IVCD (QRS interval of 112 milliseconds), and prolonged QTc interval (504 milliseconds). A serum flecainide measurement ordered on admission was available on day 2 and was 1.42 μg/mL (reference range, 0.2-0.9 μg/mL); the serum creatinine level improved to 1.6 mg/dL after intravenous fluids were administered. She was discharged on hospital day 3 and was doing well at 1-month follow-up. If AF recurs, she has opted for catheter ablation.

case_info.explanation: Atrial flutter with 2:1 atrioventricular block, and severe intraventricular conduction delay due to flecainide toxicity D. Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate Flecainide is a class Ic antiarrhythmic drug. It delays phase 0 depolarization of the action potential by blocking cardiac voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.5, resulting in slowing of conduction.1,2Its major use is in the treatment and prevention of symptomatic AF and supraventricular tachycardias. Contraindications include bundle branch block, cardiomyopathies, and significant liver or kidney impairment. The usual dose of flecainide is 50 to 150 mg every 12 hours. The half-life is 12 to 27 hours. It undergoes hepatic oxidation by cytochrome P450 (CYP2D6 isoform); however, approximately 80% of clearance is by the kidneys; thus, dosing must be reduced to 50 mg twice daily if there is kidney failure.3Notably, hemodialysis is not an effective method for clearance due to the large volume of distribution.4Aside from kidney and liver failure, toxic effects can occur with hypovolemia, hypokalemia, and hyponatremia and in patients who carry alleles that decrease their ability to metabolize CYP2D. Acute toxic effects can present with dizziness, seizures, visual disturbance, sinus arrest, atrioventricular (AV) block, and ventricular tachyarrhythmias.5Toxic effects should be suspected if the QRS duration increases by 50% or if the PR interval increases by 30%.6Prominent terminal R waves (≥3 mm) in lead aVR are a sensitive predictor of toxic effects (Figure 1).7Treatment of hemodynamically unstable tachyarrhythmias should include cardioversion. Amiodarone may be used to suppress ventricular tachycardia (VT). Bradyarrhythmias may require transvenous pacing. Closer inspection of this patient’s ECG on admission at our hospital (Figure 2) showed that the rhythm was atrial flutter (AFL) with an atrial cycle length of 230 milliseconds and 2:1 AV conduction. Flecainide slows atrial conduction, thereby slowing the rate of AFL (typically approximately 300 bpm) as seen in this patient (to approximately 260 bpm), and, if not given concomitantly with a β-blocker, may result in 1:1 AV nodal conduction resulting in ventricular fibrillation. The differential diagnosis of a wide complex tachycardia with flecainide use includes supraventricular tachycardia (including AFL) with 1:1 or 2:1 block and aberrancy, intraventricular conduction delay (IVCD), preexcitation, and VT.8 Mortality due to flecainide toxicity may be as high as 22%. The mainstay of treatment is sodium bicarbonate administration to reverse the sodium channel blockade through competitive inhibition and to alkalize the serum pH, which facilitates flecainide dissociation from its sodium channel binding sites; the pH goal should be 7.55, and the serum sodium level should be 150 mEq/L.4,9The dose is a 1-mEq/kg bolus followed by an infusion of 15 to 20 mEq/h. In refractory cases, intravenous lipid emulsion therapy may be tried—this serves as a “lipid sink” to remove lipophilic drugs, such as flecainide, from the circulation. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation may be needed in profound shock. The patient was treated with sodium bicarbonate. The QRS interval progressively narrowed with the rhythm first changing to AF and then spontaneously reverting to sinus rhythm, PR interval of 195 milliseconds, nonspecific IVCD (QRS interval of 112 milliseconds), and prolonged QTc interval (504 milliseconds). A serum flecainide measurement ordered on admission was available on day 2 and was 1.42 μg/mL (reference range, 0.2-0.9 μg/mL); the serum creatinine level improved to 1.6 mg/dL after intravenous fluids were administered. She was discharged on hospital day 3 and was doing well at 1-month follow-up. If AF recurs, she has opted for catheter ablation.
